lessons.title: Profit vs Cash: Why Reported Profit Is Not Money in the Bank

children.text: Kesari Foods earned ₹3.7 crore of profit in FY25. Over the same year its bank balance fell by ₹1.3 crore. The board approved a dividend, the auditors signed a clean report, and the company still had to draw on its cash credit line in February.

This is the most important gap in financial statements, and the one that ends businesses. Profit is an opinion about performance, built on accrual rules. Cash is a fact. This lesson shows exactly where the two separate, and how to walk from one to the other.

body.text: Profit tells you whether the business model works. Cash tells you whether the business survives the year. You need both, and only one of them pays salaries.

children.text: Six Reasons Profit and Cash Differ
Every gap between the two comes from one of six causes. Learn them and you can explain almost any cash surprise in your company.

body.caption: Where profit and cash part ways

cells: Revenue is recorded on delivery, cash arrives 60 or 90 days later
Cash is spent on stock that is not yet sold, so no expense is recorded
Cash out with no effect on profit
Expense is recorded on receipt, cash leaves weeks later
An expense is charged for assets bought in earlier years, with no cash leaving now
Cash buys a machine, which becomes an asset, not an expense
Cash out with no effect on profit
Cash moves for repayments, dividends and past-year taxes that the P&L does not carry
Cash out with no effect on this year's profit

body.text: Notice that four of the six causes have nothing to do with performance. They are timing and funding. This is why a fast-growing company is usually short of cash: growth means more receivables and more inventory, both funded before the profit is ever collected.

body.title: Spot the non-cash item
body.question: Which of these reduces profit in the P&L without any cash leaving the company this year?
options: Depreciation on a machine bought three years ago
A supplier invoice settled on the due date
body.explanation: Depreciation allocates the cost of an asset already paid for in an earlier year. The cash left the company when the machine was bought. That is why every cash flow statement adds depreciation back to profit as its first adjustment.

children.text: Walking From Profit to Cash at Kesari Foods
Lesson 1.1 did a rough version of this walk and deliberately ignored depreciation and tax. Here is the full bridge, in the order the cash flow statement itself uses.

body.caption: Kesari Foods FY25: from profit before tax to cash from operations (₹ crore)

cells: Charged in the P&L, no cash left the company
Interest is shown separately under financing, so it is added back here
Interest and rent earned are not operating income, shown under investing
Operating profit before working capital changes
Sales made but not collected, as distributors moved to 60-day credit
Cash spent on stock still sitting in the warehouse
Purchases received but not yet paid for
Actual payment to the tax department
The real cash the business generated

body.latex: \text{Cash from operations} = \text{PBT} + \text{Non-cash charges} - \text{Increase in working capital} - \text{Tax paid}
body.caption: The indirect method every Indian company uses

children.text: Now follow that ₹2.7 crore through the rest of the year. The company bought ₹3.5 crore of new equipment, paid ₹1.5 crore of interest and a ₹1 crore dividend, repaid ₹0.5 crore of lease obligations and drew ₹2 crore of fresh borrowing.

stats.label: Cash from operations
stats.context: After working capital and tax paid

stats.label: Cash used in investing
stats.context: The new equipment, less other income received

stats.label: Change in cash for the year

children.text: The company was profitable, invested sensibly and paid its owners, and still ended the year with less money than it started. Nothing here is fraud or mismanagement. It is the ordinary arithmetic of growth funded by credit.

body.title: Build the bridge yourself
body.prompt: A Nashik packaging company reports profit before tax of ₹9 crore, depreciation of ₹4 crore and finance costs of ₹2 crore. Receivables rose ₹5 crore, inventories fell ₹1 crore and payables rose ₹2 crore. Tax paid was ₹2 crore. What is net cash from operating activities, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹9 crore + ₹4 crore + ₹2 crore = ₹15 crore before working capital. Then minus ₹5 crore receivables, plus ₹1 crore from lower inventories, plus ₹2 crore payables = ₹13 crore. Less ₹2 crore tax paid = ₹11 crore. Falling inventory releases cash, which is why it is added.

body.title: The first adjustment
body.textWithBlank: The cash flow statement starts from profit and adds back ___, because it is an expense that involves no cash outflow this year.
body.explanation: Adding depreciation back does not mean it generates cash. It simply removes a non-cash deduction so that the starting point reflects actual cash movement.

children.text: Profitable and Broke: How It Happens
The dangerous combination is profit rising while cash from operations falls. It usually looks like one of these four patterns.
Growth on credit:
revenue and profit rise, receivables rise faster. Every new customer is funded by the company for two or three months before paying.
Channel stuffing:
sales are pushed into distributors at quarter end to hit targets. Profit is recorded, cash never arrives, and returns come back next quarter.
Inventory as a hiding place:
production continues into a slowing market. Costs sit in inventory instead of the P&L, so profit looks fine while cash drains.
Capex funded by working capital:
a plant is paid for out of the cash credit line, so the company is financing a ten-year asset with money that is repayable on demand.

columns.label: Healthy
points: Receivable days flat year on year
Capital expenditure funded from operating cash

columns.label: Fragile
points: Capital expenditure funded by short-term borrowing
Cash credit line fully drawn every month

body.label: The quality of earnings test
body.value: Cash from operations divided by profit after tax
body.context: Over a few years this ratio should average close to or above 1 for a healthy company. Infosys generated ₹35,694 crore of operating cash on ₹26,750 crore of profit in FY25, a ratio of about 1.33. A company where this ratio sits below 0.5 year after year is reporting profits it is not collecting.

body.text: One weak year proves nothing. A company building a new plant or entering a new market will legitimately consume cash. Look at three to five years together, and always ask what the cash was spent on. Cash consumed by capital expenditure is an investment. Cash consumed by receivables that keep ageing is a warning.

body.title: Why adding depreciation back does not create cash

children.text: This trips up almost every manager on first contact. Depreciation is added back to profit in the cash flow statement, which makes it look like a source of money. It is not.

The cash left the company on the day the asset was bought, and that outflow appears once, in investing activities, in that year. In every later year the P&L charges a slice of that cost as depreciation even though no money moves. The cash flow statement simply reverses the slice to get back to reality.
A useful way to hold it:
depreciation does not give you cash, it stops you from overstating how little cash you made.
The related trap:
a company with heavy depreciation often looks cash rich in a single year. It is not, because the assets being depreciated will need replacing, and that replacement is real cash.

body.title: Why are we borrowing if we are profitable?
body.scenario: You are a business unit head at a Hyderabad pharma packaging company. Revenue grew 28% this year and profit after tax rose from ₹6 crore to ₹8 crore. In the same year the company raised its cash credit limit twice and delayed two supplier payments. In the leadership meeting, the CEO asks why a more profitable company needs more borrowing.
body.prompt: How would you answer, and what would you ask finance for?
body.modelAnswer:
The answer in one line: growth of 28% consumed more cash in receivables and inventory than the extra ₹2 crore of profit generated.
The arithmetic to show:
1. At about 75 receivable days, revenue growth of 28% on a ₹60 crore base adds roughly ₹3.5 crore of receivables, funded before any of it is collected.
2. Inventory usually rises with volume as well, and often faster if the range of products has widened. Another ₹1.5 crore to ₹2 crore is plausible.
3. Against that, profit rose ₹2 crore and payables may have stretched by ₹1 crore. The gap is what the extra borrowing funded.
What to ask finance for:
4. The full cash flow statement, not just the P&L, for the last three years.
5. Cash from operations divided by profit after tax for each of those years, to see whether the gap is widening.
6. Receivable days, inventory days and payable days for each year, so the cause can be pinned to a specific line.
7. How much of this year's capital expenditure was funded by short-term borrowing rather than operating cash or a term loan.
What to propose:
8. A working capital target alongside the growth target, so sales teams are measured on collected revenue rather than billed revenue.
9. A review of credit terms for the fastest-growing customers, since they are consuming the most cash.
10. Matching funding to purpose: long-term assets on term loans, working capital on the cash credit line, and never the other way round.

body.title: Test your own company
steps: Take the last three years of profit after tax and cash from operations from your company's statements.
Divide operating cash by profit for each year and look at the trend, not a single year.
If the ratio is falling, check receivable days and inventory days for the same years.
Find how much cash went into capital expenditure and whether operating cash covered it.
Note how much of the borrowing is short-term against long-lived assets.
Write one sentence explaining the gap between last year's profit and last year's cash, in language your CEO would accept.

cards.definition: Cash generated by the core business after working capital movements and tax paid.
Starting from profit before tax and adjusting for non-cash items and working capital to arrive at operating cash.
An expense with no cash outflow this year, principally depreciation, amortisation and provisions.
The change in receivables, inventories and payables between two balance sheet dates.
How closely reported profit is backed by cash, commonly measured as operating cash divided by profit after tax.
Pushing stock onto distributors at period end to record revenue that is never collected cleanly.
Cash spent on long-lived assets. It appears in investing activities, not in the P&L.

points: Profit is built on accrual rules. Cash is a fact. The two differ for six predictable reasons.
Credit sales, inventory build-up and capital expenditure consume cash without reducing profit proportionately.
Depreciation is added back because no cash left this year, not because it generates money.
Kesari Foods earned ₹3.7 crore of profit, generated ₹2.7 crore of operating cash and still ended the year with ₹1.3 crore less in the bank.
Compare cash from operations with profit after tax over three to five years. A ratio persistently below 0.5 means profits are not being collected.
Fast growth consumes cash. Growing 28% and borrowing more can be perfectly healthy, as long as you know which line is absorbing it.

body.text: Kesari Foods, the Nashik packaging company and the Hyderabad pharma packaging business are fictional, with figures constructed for teaching. Infosys numbers are FY25 consolidated figures from screener.in. Nothing here is investment advice.
